[0] everyday_reading (E): Folk meaning: in maths and English, writing 'int[] a' reads as 'a is an array of ints', as if naming a list brings it into existence. Java rule: the declaration only creates a variable that can hold a reference to an int array; no array object or element space exists until new or an initializer creates one.
[1] misconception (M) -> DeclarationCreatesArray: wrong rule: int[] a; already makes an array that can be indexed. Right rule: The declaration only names the array variable; until new (or an initializer) creates the array, a[i] gives the compile-time error 'variable a might not have been initialized'.
[2] misconception (M) -> ArrayElementsUntyped: wrong rule: An array can hold elements of any type. Right rule: Every element of an array has the declared element type: an int[] holds only int values, a String[] only String references.
[3] misconception (M) -> ArrayBracketCountIsLength: wrong rule: The number of brackets in an array type is the array's length. Right rule: Each bracket pair adds one dimension (int[] is 1-D, int[][] is 2-D); the length is not part of the type and is fixed only when the array is created.
[4] inconsistent_trace (T) -> DeclarationCreatesArray: Points to LT: declare, then create, then initialize, in that order. Inconsistent application: the trace treats a as already created on some lines (reading a[i] straight after 'int[] a;') while requiring new on others. (here mixing in: "int[] a; already makes an array that can be indexed")
[5] misconception (M) -> ElementNameIsWholeArray: wrong rule: X[i] names the whole array, not one element. Right rule: The name a (written a[] in the book) denotes the whole array; a[i] denotes the single element at index i.

[0] names_the_element (N): Identity: a local variable declaration whose type is T[]; it introduces a name for a reference to an array whose elements have type T.
[1] states_the_rule (S): Declarative: 'T[] name;' declares an array variable of element type T (the C-style 'T name[]' is also legal); the length is not part of the type, so 'int[5] a;' is illegal.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Sequencing: 'double[] a;' only adds the variable a. In 'double[] a = new double[N];' the right side runs first (N is evaluated, the array is allocated and filled with defaults), and then the reference is stored in a.
[1] output_prediction (OP): Result: a declaration produces no value and no output. A declared but unassigned local array variable cannot be read at all, so any use of a or a[i] before an assignment is rejected at compile time.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): State transition: after 'int[] a;' the state gains a variable a with no value (not definitely assigned). No array object and no element variables exist yet.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): Composition: the declaration fixes the name and element type, and the creation must match it. 'double[] a = new double[N];' is legal, but 'double[] a = new int[N];' is a compile-time type error, because int[] does not convert to double[].
[1] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Plan/role: give one name to a whole sequence of same-type values, so a program reaches any of N values as a[i] instead of declaring N separate variables a0, a1, ...

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> DeclarationCreatesArray: Conservation: rewriting 'int[] a' as 'int a[]' keeps the meaning. Changing the element type changes which values may be stored and the default values. Deleting the creation step breaks the program at compile time.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Applicability: declare an array when a program must hold many values of one type and reach them by position. Do not use one for a single value, for values of different types, or for a collection that must grow as values arrive (a resizing structure such as ArrayList fits that case).
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: An array variable must refer to a created array before it is used (definite assignment). Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: a[i] is read or written after 'int[] a;' with no 'a = new int[n]' or initializer on every path to that use
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: All elements have the declared element type. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: a value or array of a different type is stored, e.g. 'int[] a = new double[5];' or 'a[0] = 2.5;' for an int[] a (incompatible types / possible lossy conversion)

double[] a; declares the array name and type; a = new double[N]; then creates the array.
int[] a = {1, 2, 3}; declares the array variable and creates and fills the array in one statement.
Declaring an array variable creates only a variable that holds a reference to an array; the array itself is a separate object.
An array is a data structure: one name for a sequence of values of the same type, organised by index.
